product.title: Hebrew 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 in modern Hebrew (Ivrit): every Hebrew word fully vowelled with niqqud, a pronunciation guide under each line of dialogue, word-for-word translations that show how Hebrew builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of the 22 letters and their five final forms, a niqqud table, an A1 overview of three-letter roots and binyanim, full tables of present, past, and future verbs, and a list of the most common verbs. Hebrew is kinder to English speakers than it looks: there is no "am/is/are" in the present, no "a/an", and the basic word order is the same as in English. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from verbs that change for a man or a woman to "have", which in Hebrew comes out as "there is to me".

blocks.text: Hebrew is often pictured as a very distant language: an unfamiliar script, a backward reading direction, and a name you meet more often in scripture than in conversation. That impression makes many people put off starting for years. Yet once the first page is open, what surprises learners most isn't the difficulty — it's how much turns out to be **simpler than in English**.

The language in this course is **Ivrit**, modern Hebrew: the language seven million people in Israel use to order coffee, argue in traffic, write the news, and put their children to bed. It's a close relative of Arabic — the same Semitic family, the same three-letter roots, the same right-to-left script — but it is not an ancient language half-revived. Ivrit is fully alive, with slang, loanwords, and a way of talking far more relaxed than people expect.
Three gifts for English speakers

**First, sentences without "is".** אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט is literally just "I student", and that's a complete, correct sentence. In the present tense Hebrew has no am/is/are at all — one whole layer of English grammar you simply get to drop.
**Second, no "a/an".** Hebrew has no indefinite article. סֵפֶר means "book" — "a book" or just "book", the form is the same. "The" exists (as a prefix), but "a" doesn't.
**Third, the word order you already know.** אֲנִי קוֹרֵא סֵפֶר = "I read book": subject, verb, object, just like English. Questions keep the same order too — you just raise your voice.
These aren't small comforts. They mean that from unit 1 you can build real sentences with very little machinery.
Three things that will trip you up

**First, every noun has a gender, and the verb changes too.** A table is feminine, a book is masculine. What makes Hebrew more demanding than French or Spanish: not only do the adjectives agree, but **even present-tense verbs change form depending on who's speaking.** A man says אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ, a woman says אֲנִי הוֹלֶכֶת — both mean "I'm going". English never asks this of you.

**Second, there are four words for "you".** אַתָּה (to one man), אַתְּ (to one woman), אַתֶּם (to a group), אַתֶּן (to a group of women). Choosing wrong isn't just a grammar slip — your listener hears at once that you haven't fitted the sentence to them.

**Third, there is no "have".** Hebrew has no verb "to have". To say "I have a brother", Israelis say יֵשׁ לִי אָח — literally **"there is to me a brother"**. This pattern is set up in unit 14 and used to the very last unit.
Three-letter roots: a habit you already have

Almost every Hebrew word grows from a **three-letter root**. From the root כ־ת־ב (write) come כּוֹתֵב (writes), מִכְתָּב (letter), כְּתֹבֶת (address), כַּתָּב (reporter), כְּתִיבָה (writing). It looks complicated — until you realize English does something similar with *write*: **writer, writing, written, rewrite**. You already think in cores and add-ons. What changes is where the add-ons go: English sticks them on the front and back, while Hebrew slips its vowels **between** the three letters.

blocks.title: What this course does NOT teach — and why
items: **Biblical Hebrew.** Biblical Hebrew and modern Ivrit share the script and the roots, but their grammar and vocabulary differ a great deal, much as Shakespeare's English differs from a modern newspaper — only more so. This course teaches the language of the streets of Tel Aviv. If your goal is reading ancient texts, it's still the right foundation — the script, roots, and binyanim are the same — but the next step is different.

**Handwriting (ktav).** Israelis write by hand with letter shapes different from print. At A1 what you need is print, because that's what appears on signs, screens, and in books. Handwritten forms are introduced briefly on the alphabet page, not practiced.

**Writing niqqud yourself.** This course prints full niqqud so you never have to guess how a word sounds. But you're not expected to add it yourself — adult Israelis don't write with niqqud either. Unit 12 trains you to read without it.

blocks.text: The twenty units cover the whole framework of A1 Hebrew: greeting and introducing yourself, saying where you're from and what you do, pointing at things, family and possession, numbers and prices, time and the clock, daily routines, ordering food, shopping, asking the way, the weather, talking about yesterday, making plans, and phone calls.

Each unit is one sitting: twenty to thirty minutes. The dialogues are short and deliberately sound like real conversation. Under each line comes the pronunciation, then a natural English translation, then a **literal** translation — Hebrew word order forced into English. That last line often sounds odd, and that's the point: it shows you how Hebrew thinks.
Enjoy the journey. בְּהַצְלָחָה! *(behatslakhah — good luck)*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course follows the Assimil method: instead of memorizing a list of rules and then trying to build sentences, you absorb whole sentences first and let the rules follow. That's why the order in which you work through each unit matters.
Six steps for one unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, out loud, without looking at the meaning.** All Hebrew text in this course is fully vowelled, so there's not a single word whose sound you have to guess. Sound first, meaning later.

**Reread it with the lines underneath.** The second line (small green letters) is the pronunciation, the third is natural English, the fourth (italic) is the **literal** word-for-word translation following Hebrew word order.
**Read the notes.** That's where the real substance of the course is. The notes explain why a sentence works the way it does, and almost always point out a typical learner's mistake.
**Read the grammar box**, then go back to the dialogue and find the examples. A rule you've just read sticks far better when you find the proof in the sentences yourself.

**Do the exercises on paper, not in your head.** Writing Hebrew by hand — right to left — is the fastest way to stop the reading direction from feeling backward. The answer key is at the end of the unit; cover it first.
**The next day, reread yesterday's dialogue** before starting a new unit. Five minutes. This is what separates people who finish twenty units and remember from those who finish and forget.

blocks.text: How to read the transliteration in this course

Pronunciation is written in an English-friendly spelling, not in phonetic symbols. Vowels are always "pure", as in Spanish or Italian: **a** as in *father*, **e** as in *bed*, **i** as in *machine*, **o** as in *more*, **u** as in *rule*. Five conventions to know from the start:

head: Written
Sounds like
Example
rows: like "ch" in Scottish **loch** or German **Bach** — a rasp in the throat
like "ts" in **cats**, even at the start of a word — one sound
made at the **back** of the throat, like French r, not with the tip of the tongue
a light catch in the throat, as in "uh-oh"; often barely heard
always like **e** in "bed" — never "ee", never silent; final **h** is silent

blocks.text: Capital letters in the transliteration mark the **stressed syllable** where the stress is unexpected. Hebrew usually stresses the **last syllable** — שָׁלוֹם is *sha-LOM*, not *SHA-lom*. English tends to stress earlier in the word, so this is the one pronunciation point to watch constantly.

blocks.title: If you only have ten minutes a day
items: Do **half a unit**: dialogue + pronunciation + notes today, grammar box + exercises tomorrow. Don't skip the exercises — that's what moves sentences from your eyes to your mouth.
The one thing never to skip: **rereading yesterday's dialogue**. These five minutes are worth more than an extra unit.

front.title: Alef-Bet: 22 letters and five final forms

blocks.text: Hebrew is written **from right to left**, with no capital letters, and the letters stand separately — they don't join up like Arabic. That's good news: each letter has just one shape, except for five letters that change shape **at the end of a word**.
Read this table from the right. The "Sound" column uses the same English-friendly spelling as the rest of the course.

head: Letter
Name
Sound
Notes
rows: Just carries a vowel; makes no sound itself
Dot in the middle = **b**; no dot = **v**
⚠️ Looks like ר — but its top right corner is square
At the end of a word usually silent, just marking the vowel **a**
Sounds **v**; with a dot it becomes the vowel **o** (וֹ) or **u** (וּ)
A typically Semitic sound; like "ch" in **loch**
The smallest letter; also marks the vowel **i**
The only letter that rises above the line

Dot on the right = **sh**; dot on the left = **s**

blocks.title: Five letters that change shape at the end of a word
items: The five pairs: kaf **כ** becomes **ך**, mem **מ** becomes **ם**, nun **נ** becomes **ן**, pe **פ** becomes **ף**, tsadi **צ** becomes **ץ**.

The rule is simple and has no exceptions: the final form is used **only** when the letter is the leftmost one in the word. All final forms have a long tail going down, except **ם**, which closes up tight. Example: מים (water) — the first mem is ordinary, the last becomes ם.

blocks.title: Four sets of letters most often confused
items: **ב / כ** — the base of ב has a square corner at the bottom right; כ is rounded.
**ד / ר** — ד has a corner sticking out at the top right; ר curves smoothly.
**ה / ח / ת** — ה has a gap at the top left; ח is closed; ת has a foot curling at the bottom left.
**ו / ז / ן** — ו is a straight line; ז wears a flat hat; ן drops below the line.

blocks.text: Three pairs of letters sound **exactly the same** in Israel today: ט and ת (t), ס and שׂ (s), כּ and ק (k). They used to differ; now they don't. The practical effect: hearing a word isn't enough to know how to spell it — which is why this course always shows the written form, not just the sound.

Israeli handwriting (כְּתָב, *ktav*) uses different shapes — א looks like a backward 2, ש like the letter e. You don't need it for this course, but don't be surprised if an Israeli's handwriting looks nothing like this page.

front.title: Niqqud: marking the vowels, and letting go of them later

blocks.text: Almost all of the twenty-two Hebrew letters are consonants. The vowels are written as **small dots and dashes below, inside, or above the letters** — that's niqqud. This course uses full niqqud from the first page to the last, so you never have to guess.

blocks.title: Traps that catch new readers
items: **Niqqud is read AFTER its letter, not before.** בַ = *ba*, not *ab*. It goes against the right-to-left reflex you've just built, and almost everyone stumbles over it in the first week.
**Two marks for the same sound.** patakh & kamats are both **a**; tsere & segol are both **e**. The difference is historical, not audible. Don't waste time telling them apart.

**Shva is often not pronounced at all.** כְּתֹבֶת is read *ktovet* — two consonants straight together at the start of a word, a cluster English never begins a word with. Practice slowly: *k-tovet*, not *ketovet*.

blocks.text: Now the important part, better learned now than discovered later: **Israelis don't write with niqqud.** Newspapers, signs, menus, WhatsApp messages, books for adults — all plain. Niqqud is used only in children's books, language textbooks, poetry, and scripture.

So how do they read it? Because Hebrew words grow from three-letter roots with a limited set of vowel patterns, text without niqqud is far easier to guess than it looks — just as you can read "txt msg" and know at once it's "text message". On top of that, unvowelled text usually adds ו and י as vowel markers (called **ktiv male**, full spelling): כתובת is written כתובת, שולחן is written with ו.
This course builds the bridge in **unit 12**: a full page of practice reading words you already know, this time without a single dot. Until then, enjoy the niqqud.
Personal pronouns
Present-tense verbs — always four forms

The form follows **who does the action**, not who is speaking. אֲנִי, אַתָּה, and הוּא all use the same masculine singular form — which is why the pronoun is usually said aloud, to make clear who is meant.
Adjectives — four forms, and always AFTER the noun
Prefixes that attach to the next word

head: Prefix
Meaning
Example
rows: בַּבַּיִת *babayit* — in the house, at home

blocks.text: Three tenses, one root
The **present** changes for gender & number, but not for person. The **past** and **future** are the opposite: they change for person and hardly care about gender (except for "you" and "they").
The form listed is the **infinitive** (מָקוֹר, *makor*) — the form you look up in a dictionary, like "to ..." in English. Almost all of them start with לְ.

If you've reached this page after working through twenty units, you're at full A1: you can introduce yourself, ask about prices and directions, order food, talk about yesterday, and make simple plans. That's no small thing — it's enough to get through a day in Israel without switching to English.
Three things that will raise your level most from here

items: **Stop using niqqud.** Rewrite the vocabulary of units 1–20 without a single dot, then read it again a week later. This is the biggest step from A1 to A2, and it needs no new material.

**Learn the remaining binyanim.** This course uses פָּעַל (pa'al) almost all the way, with an introduction to פִּעֵל and הִתְפַּעֵל in units 10 and 19. The others — נִפְעַל, הִפְעִיל, הֻפְעַל, פֻּעַל — are the stuff of A2.
**Listen to news for kids.** Simple Hebrew news broadcasts use vocabulary almost entirely covered in this course, at a speed you can still keep up with.

blocks.text: If you'd like to continue with a teacher, Linguo's private Hebrew classes pick up exactly where this leaves off — unit 21 onward, with a teacher who corrects your **ר** and **ח** live, two sounds no printed page can fix.
